statement: A=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 1\\0 & 0\end{matrix}\right],\quad B=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 0\\1 & 0\end{matrix}\right].\textnormal{For each positive integer N, start at }X(0)=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}.\textnormal{Repeat N cycles. solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write the symmetric matrix as }M=\begin{pmatrix}x&z\\z&y\end{pmatrix}=LL^{\mathsf T},\quad L=\begin{pmatrix}u&0\\v&w\end{pmatrix},\quad u,w>0, v\in\mathbb R.
\textnormal{First take K to be the identity. The integral factors into two positive-half-line gamma moments and one whole-line Gaussian, giving }\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(\frac{1}{2})\Gamma(1).

\textnormal{For the displayed positive definite K, use }M=K^{-1/2}NK^{-1/2}.\textnormal{On symmetric two-by-two matrices the Jacobian is }(\det K)^{-3/2}\textnormal{, while the determinant weight contributes }(\det K)^{\frac{1}{2}}.
statement: \textnormal{Let }K=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathcal P=\{(x,y,z):x>0, xy-z^2>0\}.\textnormal{Evaluate }\iiint_{\mathcal P}(xy-z^2)^{- \frac{1}{2}}e^{-(2x+2z+2y)}\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dz.\textnormal{Here }\Gamma(v)=\int_0^\infty u^{v-1}e^{-u}\,\mathrm du\quad(v>0).

analyticCertificate: Cholesky coordinates are bijective on the cone. For diagonal positive S=diag(s1,s2), the map N to SNS has coordinate factors s1 squared, s2 squared and s1*s2, so its three-dimensional Jacobian is (det S)^3. Orthogonal diagonalization preserves symmetric-coordinate volume up to sign, proving the stated congruence formula. All integrands are nonnegative; gamma parameters p+1 and p+3/2 are positive, so Tonelli and the changes of variables are legitimate. An independent identity-matrix route uses z=sqrt(xy)r and an angular beta integral.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any smooth u, the cofactor identity is }\nabla\cdot\left((\operatorname{cof}D^2u)\nabla u\right)=2\det D^2u.

\textnormal{On the unit circle u vanishes. With outward normal n and unit tangent tau, twice differentiating the boundary trace gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}D^2u\,\tau=u_n.\textnormal{Therefore the outward cofactor flux is }u_n^2.

\textnormal{For this polynomial, }u_n=-2\left[1+1\cos(2\theta)\right].\textnormal{The divergence theorem reduces the integral to }\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}4\left[1+1\cos(2\theta)\right]^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The cosine mean is zero and its squared integral is pi.}
statement: u(x,y)=(1-x^2-y^2)\left[1+1\operatorname{Re}(x+iy)^{2}\right].\textnormal{Find }\iint_{x^2+y^2\le1}\left(u_{xx}u_{yy}-u_{xy}^2\right)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

analyticCertificate: The polynomial is smooth on the closed disk, so divergence theorem applies directly. Along the unit circle, the second derivative of the boundary parametrization is minus the outward normal; the zero trace therefore gives the stated tangential Hessian relation with positive sign. Since the gradient is normal there, the cofactor flux becomes its squared normal derivative. The independent check expands the entire determinant and integrates its monomials over the disk.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any smooth u, the cofactor identity is }\nabla\cdot\left((\operatorname{cof}D^2u)\nabla u\right)=2\det D^2u.

\textnormal{On the unit circle u vanishes. With outward normal n and unit tangent tau, twice differentiating the boundary trace gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}D^2u\,\tau=u_n.\textnormal{Therefore the outward cofactor flux is }u_n^2.

\textnormal{For this polynomial, }u_n=-2\left[1+1\cos(6\theta)\right].\textnormal{The divergence theorem reduces the integral to }\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}4\left[1+1\cos(6\theta)\right]^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The cosine mean is zero and its squared integral is pi.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any smooth u, the cofactor identity is }\nabla\cdot\left((\operatorname{cof}D^2u)\nabla u\right)=2\det D^2u.

\textnormal{On the unit circle u vanishes. With outward normal n and unit tangent tau, twice differentiating the boundary trace gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}D^2u\,\tau=u_n.\textnormal{Therefore the outward cofactor flux is }u_n^2.

\textnormal{For this polynomial, }u_n=-2\left[1+2\cos(2\theta)\right].\textnormal{The divergence theorem reduces the integral to }\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}4\left[1+2\cos(2\theta)\right]^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The cosine mean is zero and its squared integral is pi.}
statement: u(x,y)=(1-x^2-y^2)\left[1+2\operatorname{Re}(x+iy)^{2}\right].\textnormal{Find }\iint_{x^2+y^2\le1}\left(u_{xx}u_{yy}-u_{xy}^2\right)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

analyticCertificate: The polynomial is smooth on the closed disk, so divergence theorem applies directly. Along the unit circle, the second derivative of the boundary parametrization is minus the outward normal; the zero trace therefore gives the stated tangential Hessian relation with positive sign. Since the gradient is normal there, the cofactor flux becomes its squared normal derivative. The independent check expands the entire determinant and integrates its monomials over the disk.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any smooth u, the cofactor identity is }\nabla\cdot\left((\operatorname{cof}D^2u)\nabla u\right)=2\det D^2u.

\textnormal{On the unit circle u vanishes. With outward normal n and unit tangent tau, twice differentiating the boundary trace gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}D^2u\,\tau=u_n.\textnormal{Therefore the outward cofactor flux is }u_n^2.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write an ellipse as }(X-c)^{\mathsf T}Q(X-c)\le1\textnormal{with Q positive definite. Opposite point pairs imply that recentering and rescaling Q can only reduce the area, so an optimum has center zero.}
\textnormal{Reflection symmetry in both axes then allows the off-diagonal entry of Q to be removed: feasibility is preserved and its determinant increases. Write }Q=\operatorname{diag}(p,q).

\textnormal{Maximize the concave logarithm of the product. If neither cap is active, the weighted terms are both one half; otherwise the smaller-coordinate cap is active. In this instance the maximizer is }p=\frac{1}{8},\quad q=\frac{1}{18}.

analyticCertificate: For opposite points ±v, averaging their quadratic inequalities gives v^TQv+c^TQc<=1. The centered ellipse with matrix Q/(1-c^TQc) contains every point and has no larger area; the denominator is positive because the point set spans the plane. Once centered, the signed corner constraints imply p*a²+q*b²+2|r|ab<=1 for Q off-diagonal r. Dropping r preserves all constraints and increases determinant pq-r². The remaining one-dimensional product on the active line is a concave quadratic, with the stated interior vertex or capped endpoint; this proves global optimality.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The Vandermonde product is the determinant of the monomial matrix. Expand both determinant factors into permutations and integrate each product separately. Relabeling one permutation leaves }I=720\det\left[\int_0^1x^{0+i+j}\,\mathrm dx\right]_{i,j=0}^{5}.

\textnormal{For this Cauchy matrix, multiplying by all denominators yields a polynomial alternating in the row parameters and separately in the column parameters. Its degree and leading coefficient give }\det G=\frac{\prod_{0\le i<j<6}(j-i)^2}{\prod_{i,j=0}^{5}(1+i+j)}.
statement: \int_{[0,1]^{6}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{6}x_i^{0}\right)\left(\prod_{1\le i<j\le6}(x_i-x_j)^2\right)\,\mathrm dx_1\cdots\mathrm dx_{6}.

\textnormal{Differentiating its differential equation shows that the derivative divided by k is the previous monic solution. Combining that identity with the equation at degree k minus one gives }P_k\prime=kP_{k-1},\qquad P_k=xP_{k-1}-\frac{k-1}{2}P_{k-2}.
\textnormal{No root can be repeated: simultaneous zero value and derivative would force the entire differential-equation solution to vanish. Define the inter-degree product over all roots of }P_k.

analyticCertificate: Coefficient comparison recursively determines a unique monic polynomial because all lower-degree coefficient multipliers 2(k-j) are nonzero. solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write H for the Hessian and cof H for its cofactor matrix. Commuting third derivatives gives the divergence identity }\nabla\cdot\bigl((\operatorname{cof}H)\nabla u\bigr)=2\det H.

\textnormal{On the boundary the tangential derivative vanishes, so the gradient equals its normal component times the outward unit normal. Twice differentiating the zero boundary trace along the unit circle gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}H\tau=u_n,\qquad n^{\mathsf T}(\operatorname{cof}H)\nabla u=u_n^2.
\textnormal{The divergence theorem therefore removes all unspecified interior values.}
\textnormal{The constant Fourier mode contributes two pi, each squared nonconstant mode contributes pi, and all mixed integrals vanish.}
\textnormal{The prescribed class is nonempty: in polar coordinates the following expression is a smooth polynomial in the Cartesian coordinates and has exactly the required boundary data.}
statement: \textnormal{Let u be any real function with three continuous derivatives on a neighborhood of the closed unit disk D. Its boundary value and outward unit-normal derivative are prescribed below. Determine the integral, which has the same value for every such u.}\quad D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le1\},\quad u|_{\partial D}=0,\quad u_n(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=1+\frac12\cos(1\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta),\qquad\iint_D(u_{xx}u_{yy}-u_{xy}^2)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy=?

The witness is polynomial because r^k cos(k theta) and r^k sin(k theta) are real/imaginary parts of (x+iy)^k; it proves the requested data are feasible.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write H for the Hessian and cof H for its cofactor matrix. Commuting third derivatives gives the divergence identity }\nabla\cdot\bigl((\operatorname{cof}H)\nabla u\bigr)=2\det H.

\textnormal{On the boundary the tangential derivative vanishes, so the gradient equals its normal component times the outward unit normal. Twice differentiating the zero boundary trace along the unit circle gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}H\tau=u_n,\qquad n^{\mathsf T}(\operatorname{cof}H)\nabla u=u_n^2.
\textnormal{The divergence theorem therefore removes all unspecified interior values.}
\textnormal{The constant Fourier mode contributes two pi, each squared nonconstant mode contributes pi, and all mixed integrals vanish.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Put the powers of each point in a row of the Vandermonde matrix. Its determinant is the product of pairwise differences.}
\textnormal{Each row has squared Euclidean norm at most the number of columns. Hadamard inequality bounds a determinant by the product of row norms.}

\textnormal{Take all distinct roots of unity of this order. Every row then has the maximal norm, and distinct rows are orthogonal because their inner product is a geometric sum with nontrivial unit ratio.}
\textnormal{Thus equality in Hadamard is attained, proving that the upper bound is the requested maximum. Here i is the imaginary unit and the bar denotes complex conjugation.}
statement: \textnormal{Choose arbitrary complex points in the closed unit disk. Repetitions are allowed. Find the greatest possible value of the displayed pairwise distance product.}\quad z_1,\ldots,z_{5}\in\mathbb C,\quad |z_j|\le1,\qquad\max\prod_{1\le i<j\le5}|z_i-z_j|^2=?

analyticCertificate: The Vandermonde determinant identity is a polynomial identity. Hadamard follows by orthogonalizing its rows and applying the fact that orthogonal projections cannot increase lengths. The row norm bound uses |z|<=1 term by term. Distinct nth roots give a geometric ratio different from one whose nth power is one, so each off-diagonal row inner product is zero. Equality is therefore achieved by a feasible configuration. The exact discriminant of X^n-1 separately verifies the resulting pair product.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Subtract the fast nullcline and normalize its deviation: }z=y-x^2,\qquad w=z/x^{4}.

\textnormal{Initially the deviation is zero. Its derivative at zero is positive, so the deviation stays nonnegative and the positive first coordinate decreases. At the upper ratio barrier, }w=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w\prime\le-1+\frac14+\frac{1}{16}<0.

\textnormal{These bounds give a global solution. If the decreasing first coordinate had a positive limit, the stable linear equation for the deviation would give a positive limiting deviation, forcing the first coordinate to decrease to zero. Thus the limit is zero.}
\textnormal{Variation of constants for this last scalar equation gives a ratio limit of one. Therefore }\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}x^{-4}=4w(t)\longrightarrow4.
\textnormal{Integrate and divide by time to obtain the requested normalized limit.}
statement: \textnormal{Let the real solution have the displayed initial data. Find the limit.}\quad x\prime=x^3-xy,\quad y\prime=-y+x^2+x^{4},\quad x(0)=\frac14,\quad y(0)=\frac1{16},\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}t^{\frac{1}{4}}x(t)=?

analyticCertificate: Positivity follows from x(t)=x(0) exp(-integral z), and the nonnegative z boundary points inward. The normalized ratio w is well-defined for finite time. The barrier calculation gives w<=2, hence bounded x,y and no finite escape. If x tends to ell>0, the stable scalar linear z equation converges to ell^(2m)/(1-2ell^2)>0, contradicting the positive limit for x. With x->0 and bounded w, the remainder in w prime=1-w+remainder tends to zero; the exponential convolution tends to zero by splitting its integral at a fixed large time. Cesaro integration of the inverse-power derivative gives the displayed limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Zero energy for the unperturbed equation gives the positive homoclinic orbit }x_h(t)=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t,\quad v_h(t)=-\sqrt2\,\operatorname{sech}t\tanh t,\quad\operatorname{sech}t=1/\cosh t.
\textnormal{For the dissipative part, substitute }u=\tanh t.\quad D=\int_{-1}^{1}2u^2\left[1+2^{1}(1-u^2)^{1}\right]\,\mathrm du=\frac{12}{5}.

\textnormal{The Fourier transform follows by setting }v=e^{2t}\textnormal{ in the exponential transform of the hyperbolic secant and evaluating the beta integral: }\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}t\cos t\,\mathrm dt=\frac\pi{\cosh(\pi/2)}.
\textnormal{Oddness removes the cosine-phase contribution of the velocity. Integration by parts supplies the sine-phase term.}
\textnormal{There are simple zeros precisely when the oscillating amplitude exceeds the positive dissipative constant. At equality the zero is tangent, but equality is still the infimum.}
statement: x\prime\prime=x-x^3+\varepsilon\left[-(1+x^{2})x\prime+A\cos t\right],\qquad A>0.\textnormal{Let }x_h\textnormal{ be the positive unperturbed homoclinic orbit with its maximum at zero, and put }v_h=x_h\prime.\textnormal{Define the first-order Melnikov function by }M_A(\phi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\left[-(1+x_h(t)^{2})v_h(t)+A\cos(t+\phi)\right]\,\mathrm dt.\textnormal{Find }\inf\{A>0:M_A\textnormal{ has a simple real zero}\}.

The Fourier beta integral has complex parameter (1+i)/2 with real part one half; Euler reflection gives pi/cosh(pi/2). Integration by parts has vanishing boundary terms. The sine function has simple intersections with a horizontal level strictly between minus one and one; equality gives a double tangency. This proves the infimum directly from the definition without invoking any finite-epsilon dynamical conclusion.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{On slow times between zero and one, energy dissipation and the elementary differential inequality give }(1+2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\le r\le1.
\textnormal{Choose a bounded periodic primitive of the mean-zero part and correct the amplitude: }G\prime(\theta)=F(\theta)-\overline F,\quad\widetilde r=r+\varepsilon r^{3}G(\theta).

\textnormal{Direct differentiation cancels the oscillating drift. With slow time }\tau=\varepsilon t\textnormal{, the corrected variable satisfies uniformly }\frac{\mathrm d\widetilde r}{\mathrm d\tau}=-\frac{1}{8}\widetilde r^{3}+O(\varepsilon),\quad0\le\tau\le1.
\textnormal{Gronwall comparison gives uniform convergence to the averaged solution }R(\tau)=\left(1+\frac{1}{4}\tau\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}.
statement: x_\varepsilon\prime\prime+x_\varepsilon+\varepsilon x_\varepsilon^{2}x_\varepsilon\prime=0,\quad x_\varepsilon(0)=1,\quad x_\varepsilon\prime(0)=0,\quad\varepsilon>0.\textnormal{Find the slow-time amplitude limit }\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\sqrt{x_\varepsilon(1/\varepsilon)^2+x_\varepsilon\prime(1/\varepsilon)^2}.

analyticCertificate: The nonnegative energy derivative gives a global bounded solution. The inequality r prime>=-epsilon*r^(2m+1) keeps r uniformly bounded away from zero for 0<=epsilon*t<=1. The amplitude/phase fields and their derivatives are therefore uniformly bounded on a fixed compact annulus. F minus its mean has a bounded smooth periodic primitive G. Differentiating the near-identity correction in original time gives -epsilon*mean(F)*r^(2m+1)+O(epsilon squared), since theta prime=1+O(epsilon) and r prime=O(epsilon). Dividing by epsilon and replacing r by the corrected radius costs only O(epsilon). The scalar averaged field is Lipschitz on the compact range; Gronwall gives an O(epsilon) error uniformly on the complete slow interval. Thus the growing observation time is covered, rather than justified by a formal pointwise average.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{On slow times between zero and one, energy dissipation and the elementary differential inequality give }(1+12)^{-\frac{1}{12}}\le r\le1.
\textnormal{Choose a bounded periodic primitive of the mean-zero part and correct the amplitude: }G\prime(\theta)=F(\theta)-\overline F,\quad\widetilde r=r+\varepsilon r^{13}G(\theta).

\textnormal{Direct differentiation cancels the oscillating drift. With slow time }\tau=\varepsilon t\textnormal{, the corrected variable satisfies uniformly }\frac{\mathrm d\widetilde r}{\mathrm d\tau}=-\frac{33}{2048}\widetilde r^{13}+O(\varepsilon),\quad0\le\tau\le1.
\textnormal{Gronwall comparison gives uniform convergence to the averaged solution }R(\tau)=\left(1+\frac{99}{512}\tau\right)^{-\frac{1}{12}}.
statement: x_\varepsilon\prime\prime+x_\varepsilon+\varepsilon x_\varepsilon^{12}x_\varepsilon\prime=0,\quad x_\varepsilon(0)=1,\quad x_\varepsilon\prime(0)=0,\quad\varepsilon>0.\textnormal{Find the slow-time amplitude limit }\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\sqrt{x_\varepsilon(1/\varepsilon)^2+x_\varepsilon\prime(1/\varepsilon)^2}.

analyticCertificate: The nonnegative energy derivative gives a global bounded solution. The inequality r prime>=-epsilon*r^(2m+1) keeps r uniformly bounded away from zero for 0<=epsilon*t<=1. The amplitude/phase fields and their derivatives are therefore uniformly bounded on a fixed compact annulus. F minus its mean has a bounded smooth periodic primitive G. Differentiating the near-identity correction in original time gives -epsilon*mean(F)*r^(2m+1)+O(epsilon squared), since theta prime=1+O(epsilon) and r prime=O(epsilon). Dividing by epsilon and replacing r by the corrected radius costs only O(epsilon). The scalar averaged field is Lipschitz on the compact range; Gronwall gives an O(epsilon) error uniformly on the complete slow interval. Thus the growing observation time is covered, rather than justified by a formal pointwise average.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At every fixed point, the field and its two partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian. Orthogonal coefficient vectors give }F\sim N(0,2),\quad F_x\sim N(0,1),\quad F_y\sim N(0,4),\textnormal{ independently; the second normal-distribution parameter is its variance.}

\textnormal{Write each sinusoidal pair in amplitude-phase form. A critical point can lie on the zero level only when the two positive amplitudes agree. Independent continuous amplitude distributions make this event have probability zero.}

\textnormal{A regular level has at most }4\textnormal{ intersections with almost every vertical line and at most two with almost every horizontal line. Integrating the absolute coordinate variations along the curves gives }\operatorname{Length}\{F=u\}\le4\pi(3).

\textnormal{Coarea therefore gives a bounded band approximation, and dominated convergence permits expectation through its zero-level limit: }\mathbb E\mathcal L=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\frac1{2\delta}\int_{[0,2\pi]^2}\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf1_{\{|F|<\delta\}}\,|\nabla F|\right]\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy.

\textnormal{Independence separates the band probability from the gradient norm. The field density at zero is }\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}.\textnormal{ If }Z_1,Z_2\textnormal{ are independent standard normals, polar Gaussian coordinates give }\mathbb E\sqrt{Z_1^2+4Z_2^2}=\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+4\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{Multiply the density, the gradient expectation, and the square area.}
statement: \textnormal{Let }A,B,C,D\textnormal{ be independent real standard-normal random variables, each with density }(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}.\textnormal{Let }\mathcal L\textnormal{ be the total Euclidean curve length of the zero set in the displayed square; counting or omitting the boundary does not affect this length almost surely. Find its expectation. The elliptic integral uses the displayed parameter convention.}\quad F(x,y)=A\cos x+B\sin x+C\cos(2y)+D\sin(2y),\quad(x,y)\in[0,2\pi]^2,\quad\mathcal L=\operatorname{Length}\{F=0\},\qquad E(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\theta}\,\mathrm d\theta.

analyticCertificate: Almost surely both sinusoidal amplitudes are positive and unequal, so zero is a regular value on the periodic torus. For any regular level, the coarea formula for coordinate projections bounds total absolute horizontal variation by 4*pi*k and total absolute vertical variation by 4*pi; arclength is at most their sum. The bound is uniform in the level and coefficients. The band coarea average consequently converges to the zero-level length and is bounded by the same constant; the finite set of critical values has Lebesgue measure zero in the level parameter. Expectation and the limit can be interchanged by dominated convergence. At a fixed point all coefficient combinations are jointly Gaussian and have the explicitly checked diagonal covariance, hence are independent. Tonelli separates the spatial integral and expectation. Polar coordinates for two independent unit normals have independent uniform angle and Rayleigh radius with the checked mean. The angular integral reduces to the defined complete elliptic integral after a quarter-period shift. No external random-field formula is taken on trust.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{\frac{1}{2}n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}
statement: \textnormal{For every positive integer }n,\textnormal{ let }P_n\textnormal{ be the monic polynomial of degree }n\textnormal{ satisfying the displayed equation. Its roots are listed with multiplicity. Find the limit.}\quad tP_n\prime\prime+(\frac{1}{2}n+1-t)P_n\prime+nP_n=0,\quad r_{n,1},\ldots,r_{n,n},\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{n+r_{n,j}}=?

analyticCertificate: Rodrigues formula is proportional to t^(-alpha)e^t times the nth derivative of e^(-t)t^(n+alpha), with alpha=cn>0. Integrating against t^j for j<n transfers all n derivatives and gives zero; boundary terms vanish at both endpoints. The standard sign-change polynomial argument then proves n distinct positive roots. At z=-1 each resolvent term has magnitude at most one and each derivative term at most one, giving the explicit uniform error bound. The negative algebraic root is excluded by S_n>=0; uniqueness on [0,1] plus compactness proves the limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The map }w=\frac z{z-1}\textnormal{ is conformal and bijective from the domain onto the circular annulus }1/3<|w|<1/2.
\textnormal{Under a conformal coordinate change, gradient length squared and area have reciprocal scale factors. Thus Dirichlet energy is unchanged.}
\textnormal{For each angle, the boundary difference is one. Weighted Cauchy-Schwarz gives }1\le\left(\int_{1/3}^{1/2}\rho\,u_\rho^2\,\mathrm d\rho\right)\ln(\frac{3}{2}).
\textnormal{Integrate over angles and discard the nonnegative angular energy. Equality is attained by }u(z)=\frac{\ln\!\left(3\left|z/(z-1)\right|\right)}{\ln(\frac{3}{2})}.
statement: \textnormal{In the complex plane define }\Omega=\left\{z:\frac1{3}<\left|\frac z{z-1}\right|<\frac1{2}\right\}.\textnormal{For real continuously differentiable functions on the closure, equal to zero on the inner ratio boundary and one on the outer ratio boundary, find the minimum of }\iint_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,\mathrm dA.

analyticCertificate: The Mobius map is injective away from its pole and its inverse has no pole on the closed target annulus, since the outer radius is below one. Cauchy-Riemann identities imply the conformal metric cancellation, independently checked through the real Jacobian. The radial lower bound holds for every angle and the displayed smooth pullback attains it with zero angular derivative.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{A candidate monotone profile is }y(t)=\frac1{1+e^{1t}},\quad y\prime=-1y(1-y).\textnormal{Substitution gives the displayed speed.}
\textnormal{To see uniqueness, write any decreasing front as }p(u)=-y\prime>0,\quad u=y\in(0,1).\textnormal{Then }p\frac{\mathrm dp}{\mathrm du}=cp-2u(1-u)(u-\frac{3}{4}).

\textnormal{The positive slope of p near zero increases strictly with c, whereas the positive coefficient of p near one decreases strictly with c. Thus if a larger speed had a second front, its p-graph would begin above the first and end below it.}

\textnormal{At any intersection of two positive phase graphs, their derivative difference equals their speed difference. A larger-speed graph therefore cannot cross from above to below. This contradiction proves uniqueness.}
statement: y\prime\prime+c y\prime+2y(1-y)(y-\frac{3}{4})=0.\textnormal{Find the unique real c for which there is a strictly decreasing classical solution with }\lim_{t\to-\infty}(y,y\prime)=(1,0),\quad\lim_{t\to\infty}(y,y\prime)=(0,0).

analyticCertificate: The verified logistic profile has both limits and gives existence. At the hyperbolic equilibria, standard stable-manifold asymptotics give p(u)/u tending to (c+sqrt(c squared+8k squared*a))/2 and p(u)/(1-u) tending to (-c+sqrt(c squared+8k squared*(1-a)))/2. These are respectively strictly increasing and decreasing in c. The crossing argument then proves uniqueness. The hyperbolic-endpoint asymptotic theorem is an explicit analytic prerequisite, not a symbolic-check claim.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{A candidate monotone profile is }y(t)=\frac1{1+e^{2t}},\quad y\prime=-2y(1-y).\textnormal{Substitution gives the displayed speed.}
\textnormal{To see uniqueness, write any decreasing front as }p(u)=-y\prime>0,\quad u=y\in(0,1).\textnormal{Then }p\frac{\mathrm dp}{\mathrm du}=cp-8u(1-u)(u-\frac{4}{5}).

\textnormal{The positive slope of p near zero increases strictly with c, whereas the positive coefficient of p near one decreases strictly with c. Thus if a larger speed had a second front, its p-graph would begin above the first and end below it.}

\textnormal{At any intersection of two positive phase graphs, their derivative difference equals their speed difference. A larger-speed graph therefore cannot cross from above to below. This contradiction proves uniqueness.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The quadratic matrix }A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 1\\1 & 4\end{matrix}\right]\textnormal{ is positive definite. The quartic terms are convex and coercive, so the global minimizer is unique. Its stationarity equation is }Az+z^{\circ3}=t v,\quad v=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\1\end{matrix}\right].
\textnormal{The implicit function theorem and odd symmetry give }z(t)=t w+t^3r+O(t^5),\quad w=A^{-1}v=\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{7}{15}\\\frac{2}{15}\end{matrix}\right],\quad r=-A^{-1}w^{\circ3}.
\textnormal{The envelope identity is }m\prime(t)=-v^{\mathsf T}z(t).\textnormal{Since A is symmetric, }-v^{\mathsf T}r=w^{\mathsf T}w^{\circ3}=w_1^4+w_2^4.
\textnormal{Integrate the cubic coefficient of the derivative, or differentiate it three times, to obtain }m^{(4)}(0)=6(w_1^4+w_2^4).
